characters.description: The outspoken leader of the Church's traditionalist faction. He opposes the late pope's reforms and favors a return to older doctrine and worship. His disciplined supporters make him a serious contender and a threat to Bellini's allies.
characters.name: Goffredo Tedesco

characters.description: A Filipino cleric serving in Baghdad whom the late pope secretly created a cardinal. He arrives immediately before the conclave with documents establishing his eligibility. Quiet and experienced in places marked by violence, he is initially unknown to nearly all the electors.
characters.name: Vincent Benítez

characters.description: The senior nun responsible for the sisters who house and serve the cardinals during the conclave. Observant and direct, she insists that information involving members of her community not be ignored merely because women are excluded from the election itself.
characters.name: Sister Agnes

characters.description: A Nigerian nun unexpectedly transferred to Rome shortly before the conclave. Her distress and her past connection with Cardinal Adeyemi create a scandal that alters the voting.
characters.name: Sister Shanumi

characters.description: A close attendant of the late pope who tells Lomeli that the pontiff had accused Tremblay of serious misconduct and removed him from his posts. His account starts Lomeli's inquiry into what happened during the pope's final days.
characters.name: Janusz Woźniak

recaps.ending: After an explosion nearby shakes the conclave, Benítez addresses the electors with calm authority, rejecting both fear and religious conflict. The divided cardinals unite around him, and he is elected pope, taking the name Innocent XIV. Once the result is secure, Benítez privately tells Lomeli that he discovered as an adult that he has internal female reproductive organs. The late pope knew this and still appointed him a cardinal; Benítez had considered corrective surgery but decided against altering the body in which he had been born. Lomeli understands that revealing the information would overturn the election and chooses to preserve Benítez's confidence. The new pope steps onto the balcony to greet the crowd, while Lomeli hears the life of Rome outside and accepts the unexpected outcome of the conclave.
recaps.in_short: Cardinal Jacopo Lomeli convenes a conclave after the pope's death. The main factions rally around liberal Aldo Bellini, traditionalist Goffredo Tedesco, Nigerian Joshua Adeyemi, and Canadian administrator Joseph Tremblay, while the little-known Vincent Benítez arrives as a secret papal appointment. Lomeli uncovers scandals that successively damage Adeyemi and Tremblay, including Tremblay's manipulation of a nun's transfer and improper financial inducements. Lomeli himself reluctantly attracts votes. After violence outside the Vatican, Benítez's appeal against fear and hatred breaks the deadlock, and he is elected as Innocent XIV. Benítez then reveals privately that he has internal female reproductive organs, a condition known to the late pope. Lomeli keeps the confidence and allows the validly elected new pope to appear before the public.

recaps.text: The pope dies suddenly, and Cardinal Jacopo Lomeli, Dean of the College of Cardinals, must arrange his funeral and the election of his successor. Lomeli is already experiencing a crisis of vocation and had asked to retire, but the late pope refused. As cardinals gather in Rome, factions form around several plausible candidates: liberal Italian Aldo Bellini, traditionalist Goffredo Tedesco, Nigerian Joshua Adeyemi, and Canadian administrator Joseph Tremblay. Vincent Benítez arrives from Baghdad with proof that the late pope secretly appointed him a cardinal, giving him the right to enter the conclave. Lomeli accepts the documentation and prepares to isolate the electors from the outside world.

The cardinals enter seclusion and voting begins in the Sistine Chapel. No faction can approach the required majority. Bellini's liberal support is softer than expected, Tedesco commands a committed traditionalist bloc, and Adeyemi and Tremblay gain attention as alternatives. Benítez receives little notice. Janusz Woźniak, an attendant close to the late pope, tells Lomeli that the pope dismissed Tremblay from all his offices shortly before dying because of unspecified misconduct. Tremblay firmly denies this. Lomeli must decide whether an unproved private statement can be allowed to influence a papal election.

Sister Agnes alerts Lomeli to a confrontation involving Sister Shanumi, a Nigerian nun recently transferred to Rome. Lomeli learns that Shanumi and Adeyemi had a sexual relationship decades earlier that resulted in a child. Their emotional meeting becomes known among the electors, ending Adeyemi's rise even though the old misconduct had remained private for years. Evidence indicates that Tremblay arranged Shanumi's unexpected transfer and thereby placed her where the scandal would erupt during the conclave. Lomeli's concern about Tremblay deepens, while the ballots remain fragmented and Bellini becomes increasingly despondent about stopping Tedesco.

Lomeli investigates the administration left by the late pope and finds that Tremblay used money and appointments to secure support among cardinals. The evidence supports the accusation that he acted improperly and engineered Adeyemi's downfall. Lomeli exposes the conduct to the conclave, destroying Tremblay's candidacy. Bellini's tactical efforts also compromise his standing, and some electors begin voting for Lomeli despite his insistence that he does not seek the office. Tedesco's bloc remains intact, leaving the conclave caught between a return to strict traditionalism and candidates weakened by ambition or scandal.

An explosion in Rome damages the conclave precinct and intensifies fear among the isolated cardinals. Tedesco responds by framing the violence as part of a religious struggle and argues for a combative Church. Benítez, drawing on service in regions devastated by conflict, answers with a call for courage, humility, and rejection of hatred. His composure gives the electors a candidate outside the disgraced factions. Support moves rapidly toward him, breaking the deadlock that had elevated Lomeli against his wishes.

The cardinals elect Vincent Benítez, who chooses the papal name Innocent XIV. Before appearing publicly, he tells Lomeli that a medical examination revealed he was born with internal female reproductive organs. He had traveled for surgery but chose not to alter his body. The late pope knew about the condition and nevertheless made him a cardinal in secret. Lomeli realizes that the disclosure could be used to challenge the election, but accepts that Benítez acted in good faith and keeps his confidence. Innocent XIV goes out to meet the crowd as the new pope, and Lomeli relinquishes control of the conclave's outcome.

characters.description: A middle-school teacher resigning after the death of her four-year-old daughter. Calm and methodical before her final class, she rejects the official finding of an accident and announces that two students in the room caused the child's death.
characters.name: Yuko Moriguchi

characters.description: A gifted student and aspiring inventor who craves public recognition. Moriguchi identifies him as the designer of the electrical device used against her daughter, while withholding his name from the class only as a formality.
characters.name: Shuya Watanabe

characters.description: A classmate drawn into Shuya's plan and identified by Moriguchi as the second boy responsible for Manami's death. Less assured than Shuya, he is highly sensitive to humiliation and to his mother's belief in his innocence.
characters.name: Naoki Shimomura

characters.description: Moriguchi's four-year-old daughter, whose body was found in the school swimming pool. Her death is the event around which every confession in the novel turns.
characters.name: Manami Moriguchi

characters.description: Manami's father, an educator known publicly for his work on HIV awareness. He and Moriguchi did not marry after learning that he carried HIV, but he remained part of Manami's life until illness kept him away.
characters.name: Masayoshi Sakuramiya

characters.description: A perceptive student in Shuya and Naoki's class who records the aftermath of Moriguchi's accusation. She refuses to join the class's ritualized persecution of Shuya and becomes one of the few people willing to listen to him closely.
characters.name: Mizuki Kitahara

characters.description: The enthusiastic teacher who takes over Moriguchi's class. Inspired by Sakuramiya's educational ideals, he tries to rescue absent Naoki through conspicuous home visits, without understanding how his efforts affect the boy or his family.
characters.name: Yoshiteru Terada

characters.description: Naoki's protective mother, convinced that her son was manipulated and that Moriguchi's revenge caused his collapse. She devotes herself to keeping him safe at home and interprets his increasing withdrawal through the image of the gentle child she remembers.
characters.name: Naoki's Mother

characters.description: Shuya's brilliant mother, whose scientific ambitions and frustration shaped his early childhood. She left the family and built a successful academic career, becoming the distant audience whose approval Shuya still seeks.
characters.name: Shuya's Mother

recaps.ending: Shuya completes his plan to turn a school ceremony into the spectacular crime he believes will finally make his mother notice him. After activating the bomb remotely, he hears no explosion at the school. Moriguchi calls and explains the remaining pieces of her revenge. The blood placed in the boys' milk was not infected; she relied on fear and on the consequences of their own characters rather than exposing children to HIV. She learned of Shuya's bomb, removed it from the school, and placed it in the university office of the mother he idolizes. An explosion reported there means that Shuya's attempt at recognition has apparently killed the person whose approval motivated it. Moriguchi presents this loss as the beginning of his moral reckoning, mirroring the loss of Manami without claiming that the two deaths can truly balance. Her final sardonic qualification introduces a last note of uncertainty, but Shuya's triumph has plainly been converted into devastation and Moriguchi has completed the revenge she designed around each boy's weakness.
recaps.in_short: Before resigning, teacher Yuko Moriguchi tells her class that students Shuya Watanabe and Naoki Shimomura killed her four-year-old daughter Manami. She claims to have put blood from Manami's HIV-positive father into their milk, setting off terror and retaliation. Classmates persecute Shuya, while Naoki withdraws at home and eventually kills his mother. Successive narrators reveal that Shuya's electrical device only stunned Manami; Naoki, believing he had failed to prove himself, deliberately drowned her. Shuya, obsessed with the scientist mother who abandoned him, embraces notoriety, kills the classmate who understands him best, and plants a bomb at a school ceremony. Moriguchi ultimately reveals that the blood was never infected. She has discovered the bomb and moved it to the university office of Shuya's mother. When Shuya triggers it, the explosion occurs there instead of at the school, apparently killing the person he most wanted to impress. Moriguchi tells him that his real lesson has only begun.

recaps.text: On her final day as a middle-school teacher, Yuko Moriguchi tells her class that the recent drowning of her four-year-old daughter Manami was not an accident. She identifies two students, initially called A and B, as responsible. Student A, the inventive Shuya Watanabe, built an electrified purse and tested it on the child in pursuit of attention. Student B, Naoki Shimomura, assisted him. Because juvenile law will protect the boys, Moriguchi has devised a private punishment. Manami's father, educator Masayoshi Sakuramiya, carries HIV. Moriguchi says she mixed his blood into the milk cartons Shuya and Naoki have just emptied, leaving them to fear infection. She explains that the virus is not spread casually and presents the act as a lesson in the value of life. The class recognizes both boys despite her nominal anonymity, and Moriguchi leaves the school after setting the consequences in motion.

Mizuki Kitahara describes the class after Moriguchi's departure. Their new teacher, Yoshiteru Terada, brings energetic optimism and reverence for Sakuramiya's ideals, unaware of the full history. Classmates turn Moriguchi's accusation into an organized campaign against Shuya, using the fear of HIV to isolate and humiliate him while pretending their conduct is morally justified. Mizuki refuses to participate and communicates with Shuya, who converts persecution into another stage for his need to be noticed. Naoki stops attending school, and Terada repeatedly visits his home in the belief that persistence will restore him. The public performance of concern intensifies the pressure on both boys rather than producing remorse. Mizuki sees that the class's cruelty and Shuya's cultivated indifference feed each other, while Moriguchi remains absent from the institution where her accusation continues to shape everyone.

Naoki's mother recounts his collapse at home. She believes Shuya manipulated her fundamentally kind son and regards Moriguchi's blood threat as the true source of the family's suffering. Naoki shuts himself away, refuses school, neglects his body, and becomes obsessed with contamination. His mother shields him from scrutiny and resents Terada's repeated visits, though she outwardly receives the teacher's encouragement. Her devotion depends on separating the child she loves from responsibility for Manami's death. As Naoki's behavior grows more frightening, she begins to see that recovery may require acknowledgment and outside intervention. Her attempt to confront the reality of what he has done destroys the refuge she built around him: Naoki attacks and kills her. The violence reveals that protection based on denial has neither healed him nor kept the family safe.

Naoki's own account corrects a central assumption about Manami's death. Shuya's device stunned the child but did not kill her. When Naoki realized she was still alive, he felt that his assigned role had left him insignificant beside Shuya. He placed Manami in the swimming pool and drowned her, turning a failed demonstration into murder. After Moriguchi's announcement, fear of infection, shame, and resentment become rituals of isolation and compulsive cleaning. Terada's visits feel like invasions, and his mother's insistence on innocence prevents Naoki from speaking honestly about what he did. When she finally moves toward admitting his responsibility and ending their seclusion, he interprets it as abandonment and kills her. His confession makes clear that he was neither merely Shuya's passive tool nor the blameless victim his mother needed him to be.

Shuya explains that his inventions and crimes have always been directed toward his absent mother, a gifted scientist whose recognition he values above ordinary affection. He wanted the purse device to make him famous enough for her to notice, and Manami became a means to that end. He takes pride in manipulating Naoki and in controlling the class's response to Moriguchi's accusation. Mizuki comes closest to understanding the abandonment beneath his performance, but when her insight threatens the identity he has constructed, he kills her. Shuya then prepares a larger act: a bomb hidden at a school ceremony, intended to kill many people and attach his name permanently to the event. He records his history and motives online, expecting his mother and the public to encounter the account after the attack. At the ceremony he initiates the device, convinced that mass death will complete his transformation into someone impossible to ignore.

The school does not explode when Shuya activates his bomb. Moriguchi contacts him and reveals that she has followed his preparations. She also removes the premise that began the class's panic: the milk contained no HIV-infected blood. Her revenge worked through suggestion, social cruelty, and the boys' own choices rather than deliberate infection. Having found the bomb, she transferred it away from the students and into the university office of Shuya's mother. News of an explosion there turns his intended triumph into the apparent death of the person whose attention motivated his inventions and murders. Moriguchi tells him that this consequence is the beginning of his reckoning, not a restoration of what she lost when Manami died. Her last, cutting retraction leaves a sliver of uncertainty around the precise claim, but the plan's essential result is clear: the school is spared, Shuya is broken by the fate of his mother, and Moriguchi completes a revenge tailored to what each killer valued most.
